questions.stem: Under IFRS 15 / ASC 606, revenue from a bundled contract (phone + 24-month service) is *most appropriately* recognised:

choices.text: entirely at the point the phone is delivered, since that's when control transfers.
evenly over 24 months across both the phone and service.
in proportion to the standalone fair values of each performance obligation — phone immediately, service over 24 months.

questions.explanation:
Step 4 of the 5-step model allocates transaction price to performance obligations in proportion to their standalone selling prices. The phone is a point-in-time obligation; the service is over-time.

**A** treats the whole contract as a single obligation — incorrect when there are distinct obligations.

**B** ignores the timing difference between the phone (point-in-time) and the service (over-time).

questions.stem: A company begins the year with 800,000 shares outstanding. It issues 200,000 new shares on 1 July and repurchases 100,000 shares on 1 October. Net income for the year is £2,100,000. Basic EPS is *closest* to:
questions.explanation:
Weighted-average shares:

- 800,000 × 6/12 = 400,000 (Jan–Jun)
- 1,000,000 × 3/12 = 250,000 (Jul–Sep)
- 900,000 × 3/12 = 225,000 (Oct–Dec)

Weighted-average = **875,000**.

$\text{Basic EPS} = 2{,}100{,}000 / 875{,}000 = £2.40$.

**A** uses ending shares (900,000 + a partial-year tweak) — incorrect.

**C** is the simple average of beginning and ending shares (~800k average) which ignores that the 200k issue was mid-year. Always **time-weight** mid-period changes.

questions.stem: A company has basic EPS of £3.00 (net income £6m, 2m shares). It has 400,000 outstanding employee options with a strike price of £25. The average share price for the year was £40. Using the treasury stock method, diluted EPS is *closest* to:
questions.explanation:
Step 1: Options are in-the-money (£25 strike vs £40 average) → potentially dilutive.

Step 2: Assumed proceeds = $400{,}000 \cdot 25 = £10{,}000{,}000$. Shares repurchased = $10{,}000{,}000 / 40 = 250{,}000$. Net new shares = $400{,}000 - 250{,}000 = 150{,}000$.

Step 3: $\text{Diluted EPS} = 6{,}000{,}000 / (2{,}000{,}000 + 150{,}000) = 6{,}000{,}000 / 2{,}150{,}000 \approx £2.79$.

Diluted < basic, confirms dilution.

**C** is the basic EPS (forgets dilution).

**A** likely results from adding all 400,000 options without netting against assumed repurchases.

questions.stem: A company changes the estimated useful life of its production equipment from 10 years to 7 years, increasing depreciation expense going forward. This change is *most appropriately* treated as:

choices.text: a change in accounting policy, applied retrospectively.
a change in accounting estimate, applied prospectively.

questions.explanation:
**Useful life is an estimate**. Updating it is a change in accounting estimate, which is applied **prospectively** — only future periods reflect the new life. No restatement of prior periods.

**A** confuses estimate with policy. A policy change would be switching depreciation methods (e.g., straight-line to accelerated), which is retrospective.

**C** is for material errors discovered after the fact — not for revised estimates.

questions.stem: Where on the income statement is a $50m loss from disposal of a discontinued business segment *most appropriately* reported?

choices.text: Embedded within operating expenses, with note disclosure.
As a separate line within continuing operations, before tax.
Net of tax, as a separate line item below income from continuing operations.

questions.explanation:
Discontinued operations are reported **net of tax** and **separately** from continuing operations. This makes it easy for analysts to derive a forward-looking continuing-operations earnings number.

**A** would obscure the non-recurring nature.

**B** describes treatment for unusual/infrequent items that are still part of continuing operations (e.g., a restructuring charge), not for discontinued operations.

questions.stem: Two retailers each have £500m revenue. Retailer X has COGS of 70% of revenue; Retailer Y has COGS of 40% of revenue. Which statement is *most accurate*?

choices.text: Retailer X has a stronger gross margin profile.
Retailer Y's gross margin is 60%, indicating either pricing power or a lower-cost product mix.
The two retailers should have similar operating margins since they have the same revenue.

questions.explanation:
Gross margin = 1 − COGS%. Retailer Y: 60%; Retailer X: 30%. Retailer Y is clearly the higher-margin business — likely either premium positioning, brand pricing power, or a cost-favoured product mix.

**A** is the opposite of correct.

**C** ignores SG&A and cost structure differences. Same revenue tells you nothing about operating margin without knowing the rest of the P&L.
